title: Tryouts
text:
The list went up on the gym door at 3:15. By 3:16, Marcus had read it four times, and his name still wasn't on it.

He walked to the bike rack without looking at anyone. Behind him he could hear the shouts of the kids who had made the team, the slap of high fives, someone's phone already ringing with congratulations.

"Marcus!" It was Coach Delgado, jogging across the parking lot, clipboard under her arm. "Hold on a second."

He kept his eyes on his bike lock. "I saw the list."

"I know. That's why I'm here." She caught her breath. "You were the hardest cut I had to make. Your defense is already good. Your shooting isn't there yet."

"So I'm not good enough."

"So you're not good enough yet," she said. "That's a different sentence." She tore a sheet from her clipboard and handed it to him. It was a list of drills, written in her slanting handwriting, with numbers next to each one. "Fifty of each, every day. The court by the library is open until eight. Tryouts are again in January."

Marcus looked at the paper for a long time. Then he folded it carefully, the way you fold something you plan to keep, and slid it into his jacket pocket.

That evening, the court by the library was empty except for one boy and a basketball, and the sound of the ball against the rim, over and over, until the lights came on.

title: Ode to My Old Sneakers
text:
O faithful shoes, you smell like defeat
and also like victory, and also like feet.
You carried me through two winters of slush,
one summer of puddles, one foolish rush
across a muddy field where I lost
the championship game, but gained, at a cost,
a story I still tell.

Your laces are knotted in ways no one taught.
Your soles have grown thin as a second thought.
My mother says, "It's time," and holds out a bag.
She does not understand that every rip and sag
is a map of where I've been.

So I'll wear you one more week,
one more mile, one more muddy creek,
and then I'll set you by the door
and buy new shoes that know nothing more
than the inside of a box.

title: The Shoebox (a scene from a play)
text:
[A small kitchen. Evening. ANNA, 16, sits at the table sorting through a shoebox of old photographs. Her older brother DANIEL, 22, enters carrying a suitcase. He sets it down but does not take off his coat.]

DANIEL: You're still doing that?

ANNA: (not looking up) Someone has to. Grandma kept every picture she ever took. She labeled them all. Look—"Lake Erie, 1971. Too cold to swim. Swam anyway."

DANIEL: (glancing at his watch) The lawyer said we could sell the house as is. Furniture, boxes, all of it. A company comes and clears it out.

ANNA: (setting down the photo) And the pictures?

DANIEL: Take what you want. I don't have room in my apartment for a museum.

ANNA: It's not a museum. It's her.

[A pause. DANIEL looks at the box for the first time. He picks up a photograph, turns it over, and reads the back.]

DANIEL: (quietly) "Daniel, age six. Wants to be an astronaut. Still might." (He sits down slowly, still holding it.) I don't remember this.

ANNA: She did.

[DANIEL takes off his coat and drapes it over the back of the chair. He pulls the shoebox toward him.]

DANIEL: Okay. Show me Lake Erie.

title: The Garbage Patch Is Not an Island
text:
You may have heard of the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, a huge area of ocean trash between Hawaii and California. Many people imagine it as a floating island of bottles and bags so thick that you could walk on it. The truth is different—and in some ways, more worrying.

Ocean currents in the North Pacific move in a giant circle called a gyre. Trash that enters the ocean is slowly pulled toward the center of this gyre, where the water is calmer, and it collects there. The patch formed this way over many decades.

Most of the pieces of plastic in the patch are tiny. Sunlight and waves break plastic into smaller and smaller bits called microplastics, many smaller than a grain of rice. Much of this plastic floats just below the surface, so the water can look almost clear from a ship. That is one reason the patch cannot be seen in satellite photos.

Microplastics are hard to clean up because they are so small and so spread out. They are also easy for animals to swallow. Fish, seabirds, and turtles may mistake plastic for food, and tiny pieces can move up the food chain.

Scientists and engineers are testing ways to collect large floating debris before it breaks apart. But most experts agree that the best solution starts on land: keeping plastic out of the ocean in the first place.

title: What the Lifeboats Tell Us
text:
When the RMS Titanic sank in the North Atlantic on April 15, 1912, more than 1,500 people died. The ship had struck an iceberg late the night before, and less than three hours later it was gone. For more than a century, people have asked how such a disaster could happen to a ship that was celebrated as a marvel of engineering.

One answer lies in the lifeboats. The Titanic carried about 2,200 people, but its lifeboats had room for only about 1,178. This was not illegal. British safety rules at the time based the number of lifeboats on a ship's weight, not on the number of people aboard, and the rules had not been updated for ships as large as the Titanic. In fact, the Titanic carried more lifeboats than the law required.

Making matters worse, many lifeboats were lowered only partly full. In the confusion, some passengers did not believe the ship was really sinking, and the crew had never practiced a full evacuation. Some boats left with fewer than half of their seats filled.

The disaster led to major changes. In 1914, nations signed the first International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea, which required enough lifeboat space for everyone on board, regular lifeboat drills, and a radio watch around the clock. Rules that grew out of this agreement still shape ship safety today.

The Titanic is often remembered as a story about an iceberg. It may be more accurate to remember it as a story about rules that had not kept up with technology.

title: Should Zoos Exist? Two Views
text:
VIEWPOINT 1: Zoos Are Arks for Endangered Species

Modern zoos are not the cramped animal prisons of the past. Accredited zoos today run breeding programs for endangered species, carefully matching animals to keep populations healthy. Some species survive today largely because of these programs. The Arabian oryx, for example, was hunted to extinction in the wild by the early 1970s; animals bred in captivity were later released, and wild herds now live in the Middle East again.

Zoos also teach. Millions of visitors each year see animals they would otherwise only read about, and many leave caring more about protecting wildlife. A child who watches a gorilla up close may grow into an adult who supports conservation.

VIEWPOINT 2: The Wild Cannot Be Replaced

Even the best zoo enclosure is a tiny fraction of an animal's natural range. Elephants in the wild may walk many kilometers in a day, and polar bears roam enormous territories. In captivity, some animals develop repetitive behaviors, such as pacing back and forth, that scientists consider signs of stress.

Supporters point to success stories like the oryx, but only a small share of the animals in zoos belong to endangered species. Many are kept mainly because visitors enjoy seeing them. If the true goal is saving species, money might do more good protecting habitats in the wild, where entire ecosystems can be preserved at once.

title: The Puzzle of the Placebo
text:
In medical research, a placebo is a treatment with no active ingredient—a sugar pill, for example, or an injection of salt water. Placebos are used in experiments to test new medicines. One group of patients receives the real drug and another receives the placebo, and researchers compare the results. If the drug works better than the placebo, it is considered effective.

But placebos have a strange habit of working. In study after study, some patients who take a sugar pill report real improvements, especially for symptoms such as pain, nausea, and fatigue. This is known as the placebo effect, and it has puzzled doctors for decades.

Part of the explanation is expectation. When people believe a treatment will help, the brain can change how it processes signals such as pain. Brain-imaging studies have found that patients taking placebos can show activity in some of the same brain regions involved in the body's natural pain relief. Ritual matters, too: the attention of a caring doctor, the formality of a prescription, even the color and size of a pill can influence how patients respond.

Some researchers have tested an even stranger idea: "open-label" placebos, in which patients are told directly that they are receiving a pill with no medicine in it. In several small studies, patients still reported feeling better.

None of this means that placebos can cure diseases. They do not shrink tumors or kill bacteria, and relying on them instead of real treatment can be dangerous. Their effects are mostly limited to how people feel, not to the underlying illness. Still, the placebo effect is a reminder that healing is not only chemical. What patients expect, and how they are treated, can shape their experience of illness.

title: The Woman Who Mapped the Ocean Floor
text:
In the early 1950s, most scientists pictured the deep ocean floor as a flat, featureless plain covered in mud. Almost no one had seen it, and the tools to measure it were limited. That picture changed largely because of a geologist named Marie Tharp, who did not set foot on a research ship during the first years of her work.

At the time, women were not allowed to join research voyages at Tharp's institution. Instead, her colleague Bruce Heezen went to sea and collected echo soundings—measurements of depth made by bouncing sound off the sea floor. Tharp stayed in the lab, turning thousands of these measurements into detailed drawings of the landscape beneath the Atlantic Ocean.

As she worked, Tharp noticed something unexpected. Running down the middle of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, an underwater mountain range, was a deep valley. She believed it was a rift—a place where the Earth's crust was being pulled apart. This supported the controversial idea of continental drift, which held that the continents slowly move. Heezen initially dismissed her interpretation, and many geologists of the era rejected continental drift entirely.

But the evidence kept accumulating. When the locations of underwater earthquakes were plotted, they lined up along Tharp's rift valley. By the late 1960s, the theory of plate tectonics—which explains how the Earth's outer shell is divided into moving plates—had become the foundation of modern geology, and Tharp's maps were among its most persuasive evidence.

In 1977, Tharp and Heezen published a map of the entire world's ocean floor, revealing a planet-spanning system of ridges, trenches, and rifts. Recognition for Tharp's role came slowly; for years, her name appeared after Heezen's, if at all. Today, she is widely credited as one of the scientists who made plate tectonics visible—proof that a discovery can come from careful attention to data as much as from adventure.
